headline: Sabi's Mind-Reading Beanie Promises Thought-to-Text Without Surgery
lede: A California startup called Sabi wants to make the surgeon optional. Its product, the Sabi Cap, is a knitted beanie lined with up to 100,000 custom biosensors that record the brain's electrical activity through the scalp — no incision, no implant. The company claims its artificial-intelligence system can translate *internal speech* into typed text at roughly 30 words per minute, a figure that, if verified, would exceed anything demonstrated in the peer-reviewed literature.
body:
The cap uses *electroencephalography* (EEG), which measures the brain's electrical activity via electrodes placed on the scalp. Conventional research-grade EEG systems run on 64 to 512 channels; clinical devices typically use 19 to 64. Sabi's claimed 70,000 to 100,000 sensors would represent a roughly 200-fold increase over the research frontier. The company has not published a methods paper. It says it uses custom in-house silicon chips to power the dense array, and that a proprietary **Brain Foundation Model** — a class of neural-data AI analogous to large language models, trained to generalize across individuals rather than calibrate to each user — was built on 100,000 hours of EEG recordings from 100 volunteers.

The term *brain foundation model* is not Sabi's coinage. A March 2025 survey in IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering formally defined the category, drawing on several years of published work: EEGPT, BrainLM, and Brain-JEPA are peer-reviewed examples. The approach pre-trains a large neural network on diverse recordings, then fine-tunes for specific tasks — the same recipe as BERT or GPT-style language models. Where the field has not arrived is continuous *imagined-speech* decoding at practical speeds. The best published EEG imagined-speech studies classify roughly 33 to 36 percent accurately across five or six word categories — not a continuous speech channel, and far short of 30 words per minute.

The comparison to **AlphaFold** — DeepMind's (Alphabet (GOOGL)) system that cracked a 50-year protein-folding problem, was independently verified at a blinded international benchmark before any milestone was claimed, and contributed to the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — is structurally premature. AlphaFold submitted to an external evaluation with ground-truth answers and published full methods in *Nature*. Sabi has published no paper, submitted to no benchmark, and no independently conducted demonstrations appear on the public record. There is also a physics-based constraint the protein-folding problem did not carry: skull and scalp tissue attenuates and spatially smears neural signals before they reach any surface electrode. Packing more sensors onto the scalp improves spatial sampling but does not restore information already lost to tissue — a ceiling that sensor count alone cannot lift.

Sabi's funded rivals illuminate the difficulty. Synchron's *Stentrode* — an *endovascular* implant that threads electrodes through a blood vessel near the motor cortex, bypassing the skull entirely — achieves 5 to 10 words per minute in clinical trials with just 16 electrodes. Neuralink's N1 implant uses 1,024 *intracortical* electrodes drilled into brain tissue and has demonstrated precise motor decoding, though no typing-speed figure has been published. The most directly comparable verified benchmark comes from Meta Platforms (META): its neural wristband, which reads *surface electromyography* (*sEMG*) — electrical signals from forearm muscles rather than the brain — achieved 20.9 words per minute in a peer-reviewed *Nature* paper in July 2025. That result used a far cleaner signal than scalp EEG. If Sabi's cap genuinely exceeds it without touching the skin below the neck, the implication would be extraordinary.

Khosla Ventures, whose founder the tweet quotes approvingly, has hedged its own position: the firm also backed Synchron (invasive, *endovascular*) and Paradromics (invasive, *intracortical*), suggesting conviction in the BCI category rather than a committed view that non-invasive is the inevitable winner. Sabi's training-data figure deserves its own scrutiny: 100,000 hours of EEG from 100 volunteers implies roughly 1,000 hours of recording per person — approximately six months of continuous wear each — a number that strains credulity without clarification of whether augmented or synthetic data is included. The company says the cap will ship by end of 2026. The real measure of the AlphaFold analogy is not whether the product ships; it is whether, when it does, an independent neuroscientist can sit down, don the beanie, and type a sentence by thinking it — with no company representative curating what is shown.

concepts.definition: A technique for recording the brain's electrical activity by placing electrodes on the scalp. Signals must pass through skin and bone before reaching the sensors, which attenuates and spatially blurs them — a fundamental physical limitation compared with implanted devices that sit directly on or inside brain tissue.

A system that reads neural signals and translates them into commands for an external device — a cursor, keyboard, or robotic limb — without requiring physical movement. BCIs can be invasive (electrodes implanted in or on the brain) or non-invasive (reading signals through the scalp).

A large AI model pre-trained on diverse EEG or other neural recordings from many subjects, then fine-tuned for specific tasks such as imagined-speech decoding. The approach mirrors how large language models like BERT are pre-trained on broad text corpora and adapted for downstream tasks. Formally defined as a research category in a March 2025 IEEE survey, with peer-reviewed examples including EEGPT, BrainLM, and Brain-JEPA.

The mental rehearsal of words without audible vocalization or perceptible muscle movement — sometimes called inner speech or subvocalization. Decoding imagined speech from brain signals is considerably harder than decoding overt speech or motor intentions, because the neural patterns are subtler and more variable across people and sessions.

A technique that records the electrical signals produced by muscles — in Meta's wristband, the forearm muscles involved in fine finger movements. Because muscle signals are much stronger and less noisy than scalp EEG signals, sEMG-based interfaces have achieved higher decoding accuracy with far less data and compute.

A surgical approach that accesses the brain via blood vessels rather than open craniotomy. Synchron's Stentrode is threaded through the jugular vein into a vessel near the motor cortex, making it less invasive than drilling through the skull while still placing electrodes far closer to neurons than any scalp device can achieve.

Describes electrodes physically inserted into the brain tissue (cortex) itself. Intracortical arrays — like Neuralink's N1 and Paradromics' Connexus — capture the strongest and most spatially precise neural signals but require neurosurgery and carry ongoing risks of infection and tissue reaction.

Synchron's proprietary endovascular BCI electrode array. Deployed by threading it through the superior sagittal sinus — a blood vessel near the motor cortex — it unfurls against the vessel wall to record nearby neural activity, eliminating open-brain surgery while keeping sensors far closer to neurons than scalp EEG permits.

A deep-learning system developed by DeepMind that in 2020 effectively solved the protein-structure prediction problem — determining how a protein folds into its three-dimensional shape from its amino acid sequence alone, a challenge that had stumped biology for 50 years. Its performance was verified at the independent CASP14 competition before any milestone was claimed, and its co-creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

fact_check: Two of Sabi's headline claims invite scrutiny. First, the training-data figure — 100,000 hours of EEG from 100 volunteers — implies roughly 1,000 hours of recording per person, or approximately six months of continuous wear each; Sabi has not clarified whether this figure includes augmented or synthetic data. Second, the claim of 30 words per minute for continuous imagined-speech decoding from scalp EEG has no peer-reviewed equivalent: the best published EEG imagined-speech studies achieve multiclass classification accuracy of around 33–36 percent across five to six word categories, not continuous speech output at any measured speed. Neither claim has been independently verified by external researchers, and Sabi has published no methods paper.
